message:
Please review the following document.

<document>
# Memo

**To:** Director of Operations, Brookside Veterinary Group
**From:** [Analyst]
**Date:** 13 November 2026
**Re:** Evening and Saturday hours pilot at 3 clinics in 2027

## Recommendation

**No-go on the pilot as proposed.** Instead, approve a smaller test: Saturday-only hours at one northern-suburbs clinic from April 2027. Expand only if that test meets clear volume targets.

## Why not the full pilot

**1. The volume needed to break even is higher than the evidence supports.**
- Each clinic would add 28 hours a week at about $310 an hour, or $8,680 a week.
- Each urgent visit contributes about $204 ($340 × 60%).
- Each clinic therefore needs about 43 visits a week, or 1.5 per open hour, just to cover staffing.
- Across 3 clinics, that is about 550 visits a month.

The after-hours phone line receives 1,140 calls a month for all 9 clinics. About 730 of those (64%) are treatable urgent cases. However, many of those calls come overnight, on Sundays or on holidays, which the pilot would not cover. Some are repeat calls about the same pet, and not every caller would drive to one of only 3 open clinics. Breaking even would require converting roughly three-quarters of all treatable after-hours calls across the network into pilot visits. That is implausible without substantial new demand, and we have no evidence of that demand. At full scale, the pilot commits about $1.35 million a year in staffing before any vet pay premium.

**2. We cannot staff it reliably.**
- We already have 4 unfilled veterinarian positions.
- 70% of current veterinarians will not work regular evenings.
- Evening recruits expect a 20–25% premium, which raises the break-even volume further.
- The pilot needs about 84 veterinarian-hours a week, roughly two full-time vets. Pulling existing vets onto evening shifts would worsen daytime gaps.

**3. It puts an existing referral stream at risk.**
Valley Animal Emergency sends us about 300 follow-up patients a year, and its owner has signalled she may reconsider this. Losing those referrals would partly offset any gains, and that loss would begin before the pilot proves itself.

## Why not do nothing

The demand signal is real. 72% of clients say they would prefer to come to us for urgent care. A competitor has opened two urgent-care clinics in the past year. If we wait, we risk giving up this market permanently.

## Proposed smaller test

- **Saturday hours, 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., at one northern clinic.** Six of our 9 clinics are in the northern suburbs, so most of our clients are there.
- **Cost:** about $2,500 a week, or roughly $130,000 a year. Break-even is about 12 visits per Saturday.
- **Staffing:** covered by the roughly 30% of vets willing to work extra hours, paid at a premium, with no new hires needed.
- **Before the end of the month:**
  - Log after-hours calls by hour and day.
  - Record each caller's nearest clinic.
- **Before launch:** meet Valley's owner to agree on what cases each side handles. One option is to keep referring overnight and true emergency cases to Valley.
- **Expansion trigger:** if Saturday visits average 15 or more over 3 months, extend to evenings at the same clinic, then to a second site.

This approach tests real demand at about a tenth of the cost and protects the Valley relationship. It also gives us a defensible basis for a larger decision in late 2027.

---

##
</document>
response:
# Review: Evening and Saturday Hours Pilot Memo

This is a strong memo. The recommendation comes first, the reasoning is quantified, and the alternative is concrete. The arithmetic checks out. The main weaknesses are in the smaller test itself, which gets less scrutiny than the full pilot does.

## Arithmetic check

| Claim | Check | Result |
|---|---|---|
| 28 hrs × $310 = $8,680/week | ✓ | Correct |
| $340 × 60% = $204 | ✓ | Correct |
| ~43 visits/week, 1.5/hour | 8,680 ÷ 204 = 42.5; 42.5 ÷ 28 = 1.52 | Correct |
| ~550 visits/month across 3 clinics | 42.5 × 3 × 4.33 ≈ 552 | Correct |
| 730 of 1,140 calls = 64% | 64.0% | Correct |
| "Roughly three-quarters" of treatable calls | 552 ÷ 730 = 76% | Correct |
| ~$1.35M/year | 8,680 × 3 × 52 = $1,354,080 | Correct |
| 84 vet-hours ≈ 2 FTE | 28 × 3 = 84 | Correct |
| Saturday test ~$2,500/week, ~$130K/year | 8 × 310 = $2,480; × 52 = $128,960 | Correct |
| Break-even ~12 visits/Saturday | 2,480 ÷ 204 = 12.2 | Correct |
| "About a tenth of the cost" | 129K ÷ 1.35M = 9.5% | Correct |

## Substantive issues

**1. The smaller test's break-even leaves out the premium.**
The memo says Saturday vets will be "paid at a premium." But the $2,500 cost and the 12-visit break-even use the base $310 rate. A 20–25% premium on the vet share of that rate pushes break-even to roughly 13–15 visits. That puts it at or near the 15-visit expansion trigger, so the trigger may only mean "breaking even," not "proven demand." Restate the cost with the premium included, and set the trigger clearly above the adjusted break-even.

**2. "30% willing to work extra hours" is an inference, not a finding.**
The data says 70% *will not work regular evenings*. That does not mean the other 30% will work Saturdays, and that 30% may also include vets who are already stretched by the 4 vacancies. Either confirm actual Saturday volunteers before committing, or soften the claim.

**3. "Six of 9 clinics are in the north, so most clients are there" doesn't follow.**
The number of clinics is not the same as client share. The call-logging step will help, but site selection should rest on client addresses or caller-location data, not clinic count.

**4. The central demand argument is unquantified.**
The case against the full pilot depends on how many of the 730 calls fall in pilot hours. The memo says "many" come overnight or on Sundays but gives no figure. If even rough data exists, include it. If not, say plainly that this is an assumption. The logging step shows you know this gap exists, so name it in the argument too.

**5. There is no stop rule.**
The test has an expansion trigger but no exit condition. Add one, for example: "If Saturday visits average below X after 3 months, discontinue." This makes the $130K commitment visibly bounded, which strengthens the "defensible basis" claim.

**6. The logging window is short.**
From 13 November to month-end is about 2.5 weeks of November data, which is thin and possibly seasonal. Consider continuing the log through launch so you have baseline data for April.

**7. Smaller points:**
- **Cannibalization:** the break-even assumes every pilot visit is new revenue. Some will be visits shifted from weekday slots. This strengthens your case against the full pilot, so mention it.
- **Valley referrals:** 300 patients a year is unquantified in dollars. One line estimating their contribution would let the reader weigh the risk.
- **The 72% figure:** this is stated preference. Treat it as a signal, not a demand forecast. The wording "the demand signal is real" slightly overstates it.
- **Saturday to evenings:** Saturday demand may not predict weekday-evening demand, so the expansion path assumes some transferability. Consider whether evenings need their own trigger.

## Formatting and cleanup

- **Remove the empty `##` heading** at the end of the document.
- **Replace the `[Analyst]` placeholder** with a name.
- **Consider reframing the headline.** "No-go on the pilot as proposed" is accurate, but the actual ask is a go on a smaller test. Something like "**Recommend a smaller test instead of the 3-clinic pilot**" leads with the action you want approved.

## Bottom line

The case against the full pilot is well made and numerically sound. Before sending, fix the premium in the Saturday break-even (issue 1), confirm vet availability (issue 2), and add a stop rule (issue 5). Those three changes would make the alternative as rigorous as the rejection.
